hops.title: Frog axons steer toward softer brain tissue
hops.text: A growth cone pulls on what it grips, so firmness matters to it. In 2016 a University of Cambridge team pressed a tiny probe against the brains of living frog embryos and mapped how squishy each region was. The young visual pathway ran through stiffness gradients, and retinal axons turned away from stiffer tissue toward softer tissue. Many other cell types, given a choice in a dish, crawl toward the stiffer side. Then the team pressed a bead onto one spot for about six hours, which stiffens brain tissue. The axons never grew right under it, and in three of five embryos they swerved away from it or around it.

sources.citation: Koser, D. E. et al. (2016). Mechanosensing is critical for axon growth in the developing brain. Nature Neuroscience 19:1592-1598.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A smiling scientist and a small frog on a lab bench look at two blocks of gelatin, one firm and one being gently dimpled by a thin probe tipped with a bead.
image.caption: In living frog embryos, retinal axons turned away from stiffer brain tissue and grew toward softer tissue.

hops.title: Blindfolded volunteers tracked a chocolate trail by smell
hops.text: In a 2006 study, UC Berkeley researchers soaked a 10-meter string in chocolate essence and laid it in the grass outside Barker Hall. Volunteers in opaque masks, earmuffs, knee and elbow pads and work gloves crawled along it, zigzagging the way tracking dogs do. Two-thirds of the 32 reached the end within three tries. Your nostrils sample air from spots about 3.5 centimeters apart. Four trained trackers then wore a nasal "prism" that fed both nostrils air from one spot. They finished 5 of 12 runs, compared with 9 of 12 using a control prism with separate inlets. They could still smell the chocolate; they had lost the comparison.

sources.citation: Porter, J. et al. (2007). Mechanisms of scent-tracking in humans. Nature Neuroscience 10:27-29.
Sanders, R. (18 December 2006). Two nostrils better than one, researchers show. UC Berkeley News.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A blindfolded volunteer in coveralls, earmuffs and gloves crawls across a campus lawn along a winding string while a dog watches.
image.caption: Volunteers tracked chocolate by smell; giving both nostrils the same air cut successful runs from 9 to 5 of 12.

hops.title: Did a growth cone crawl the length of a blue whale?
hops.text: By one estimate, some spinal axons in a blue whale reach about 30 meters. It is tempting to picture a growth cone crawling that whole way. But at the few millimeters a day that axons typically regrow after a peripheral nerve injury, 30 meters would take decades. Researchers think the growth cone does its steering early, while the embryo is small, and then the growing body stretches the connected axon. At the whale's peak growth, that stretch is estimated at about 3 centimeters a day, which would add roughly one and a half times the volume of the nerve cell's body every day.

sources.citation: Smith, D. H. (2009). Stretch growth of integrated axon tracts: extremes and exploitations. Progress in Neurobiology 89:231-239.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A blue whale and its calf swimming side by side through sunlit ocean.
image.caption: A blue whale's longest axons are thought to lengthen mostly by being stretched as the body grows.

audio.title: A blue whale, a chocolate trail and a Nobel quarrel
audio.transcript:
Growth cones are tiny, about ten micrometers across in a dish, but they turn up in some wonderfully odd stories. Here are three.

First, the blue whale. By one estimate, some of the spinal axons in a blue whale reach about thirty meters, longer than a basketball court. So did a growth cone crawl all that way? Almost certainly not. After a peripheral nerve injury, regrowing axons manage only a few millimeters a day on average. At that pace, thirty meters would take decades. Researchers think the growth cone does its steering early, while the embryo is still small, and finds its partner. After that, the growing body stretches the connected axon. At the whale's peak growth, that stretching is estimated at about three centimeters a day, which would add, by a rough estimate, about one and a half times the volume of the nerve cell's body every single day. In the lab, a team at the University of Pennsylvania used a small motor to stretch connected axons in a dish out to ten centimeters without breaking them. Axons stretched to five centimeters were, on average, thicker than unstretched ones, not thinner.

Second, a chocolate trail. In December two thousand six, researchers at U C Berkeley reported an experiment that began with a ten-meter string soaked in chocolate essence and laid in the grass outside Barker Hall. The volunteers wore opaque masks, earmuffs, knee and elbow pads and work gloves, so smell was the only clue, and crawled along on all fours. Two-thirds of the thirty-two volunteers followed the scent to the end within three tries, zigzagging across the trail the way tracking dogs do. Your two nostrils sample air from spots about three and a half centimeters apart. So the team built a nasal prism that fed both nostrils air from a single spot, leaving no difference between them. Four trained trackers wearing it finished only five of twelve runs, compared with nine of twelve when a control prism kept the two inlets apart. They could still smell the chocolate, but they had lost one way of telling which side it was stronger on. A growth cone in the pipette assay works on a far smaller scale, reading a cue only five to ten percent stronger on one side.

Third, a Nobel Prize shared by two men who disagreed. In December nineteen oh six, Camillo Golgi and Santiago Ramón y Cajal shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for their work on the structure of the nervous system. On December eleventh, Golgi began his Nobel lecture by saying he had always been opposed to the neuron theory, the idea his co-winner championed. The next day it was Cajal's turn. Among his pictures were growth cones from chick embryos, stained with his own silver method and with Golgi's. It would be very convenient, Cajal said, if the nerve centers were one continuous network. Unfortunately, nature seems unaware of our intellectual need for convenience and unity. He also admitted something honest: their claims could go no further than the methods of the day. Both men were reading dead, stained tissue. The next year, in nineteen oh seven, Ross Harrison kept a piece of frog embryo alive in a drop of clotted lymph and watched nerve fibers grow out of it, their tips moving as they went. In some of his cultures he could see a fiber growing from a single cell.
